title: Speeches, Reports and Formal Letters
summary: Writing and delivering speeches, the format of formal reports and newspaper reports, and formal letters to the press and of application, with register and structure.

notes.text: A **speech** is written to be **heard**, so it must be clear, engaging and easy to follow. It should suit the **audience**, **purpose** and **occasion** (e.g. a farewell, a prize-giving, a campaign speech for the RCL).

items: **Greeting**: acknowledge the audience ('Good morning, Principal, teachers and fellow learners').
**Introduction**: grab attention with a question, quotation, anecdote or surprising fact, and state your topic.
**Body**: three main points, each with examples.
**Conclusion**: summarise and end memorably, e.g. with a call to action.

notes.caption: Rhetorical devices for speeches
rows: 'We must learn, we must lead and we must serve.'
'What kind of school do we want to leave behind?'
'You, the Grade 9s, are the leaders of tomorrow.'

notes.label: Delivery tips
notes.text: Make eye contact, speak clearly and not too fast, vary your tone, use cue cards rather than reading every word, and stand confidently.

notes.title: A strong opening
notes.problem: Improve: 'Today I will talk about littering.'
steps: Grab attention with a question, fact or image.
notes.answer: 'Fellow learners, look at the ground around you. Is this the school we are proud of?'

notes.text: A **formal report** gives factual information about an investigation or event to a specific reader (e.g. a report to the principal on littering at school). It is objective, uses formal language and is often written in the passive voice and the past tense.

rows: Who asked for the report and why
How the information was gathered (surveys, interviews, observation)
The facts discovered, often under numbered sub-headings
Name and position of the writer

items: **Headline**: short and catchy, in the present tense ('Learners Plant 500 Trees').
**By-line** and **dateline**: the reporter's name, the place and date.
**Lead paragraph**: answers the **5 Ws and H**: who, what, when, where, why and how.
**Body**: further details in order of importance (the inverted pyramid), with quotations from witnesses or experts.
Written in the **third person**, objectively, in short paragraphs.

notes.title: Writing a lead paragraph
notes.problem: Facts: a fire, Monday night, Khayelitsha, 40 homes, no injuries. Write a lead.
steps: A lead answers who, what, when and where.
Put the most important fact first.
notes.answer: 'Forty homes were destroyed by a fire in Khayelitsha on Monday night. No injuries were reported.'

items: **Letter to the press**: written to a newspaper editor to express an opinion on a public issue. Begin 'Dear Editor' or 'Sir/Madam', state your view and reasons, and end 'Yours faithfully' with your name and town.

**Letter of application**: applies for a job, a bursary or a position. State the position and where you saw it, describe your relevant skills and experience, say why you are suitable, and mention attachments such as your CV.

notes.label: Remember
notes.text: Formal writing avoids slang, contractions (don't, can't) and abbreviations such as 'LOL'. Keep sentences clear and paragraphs focused.
